text_blocks.snippet: Yes, diabetes can damage your kidneys. Elevated blood sugar levels from diabetes can gradually harm the blood vessels and filtering units within the kidneys, leading to a condition called diabetic nephropathy. This damage can impair the kidneys' ability to filter waste from the blood, potentially leading to kidney failure.
snippet_highlighted_words: Yes, diabetes can damage your kidneys

list.title: Diabetic Nephropathy:
list.snippet: Diabetes can cause diabetic nephropathy, a type of kidney disease that develops over time.

list.title: Kidney Function:
list.snippet: The kidneys filter waste and excess fluid from the blood. In diabetes, high blood sugar can damage the nephrons, the filtering units within the kidneys.

list.title: Early Signs:
list.snippet: Early signs of kidney damage may include protein in the urine (albuminuria) and high blood pressure.

list.title: Advanced Stages:
list.snippet: As nephropathy progresses, symptoms can worsen, leading to fatigue, swelling, nausea, and even kidney failure.

list.title: Risk Factors:
list.snippet: Factors like poorly controlled blood sugar, high blood pressure, obesity, and certain ethnicities can increase the risk of diabetic nephropathy.

list.title: Prevention and Management:
list.snippet: Managing blood sugar and blood pressure, along with lifestyle changes like diet and exercise, can help prevent or slow down kidney damage.

list.title: Reversal:
list.snippet: While existing kidney damage cannot be reversed, early detection and management can help slow progression and potentially prevent kidney failure, according to the American Kidney Fund.

text_blocks.snippet: Diabetes can significantly impact kidney health, potentially leading to diabetic nephropathy (kidney disease) and even kidney failure. High blood sugar levels, a hallmark of diabetes, can damage the tiny blood vessels within the kidneys, impairing their ability to filter waste and excess fluid from the blood. This damage can progress over time, sometimes without noticeable symptoms in the early stages.
snippet_highlighted_words: High blood sugar levels, a hallmark of diabetes, can damage the tiny blood vessels within the kidneys, impairing their ability to filter waste and excess fluid from the blood

list.title: Damage to glomeruli:
list.snippet: The kidneys contain structures called nephrons, each with glomeruli, which are tiny blood vessels that filter blood. High blood sugar can damage these glomeruli, making them leaky or scarred.

list.title: Proteinuria:
list.snippet: When glomeruli are damaged, protein, particularly albumin, can leak into the urine, a condition called proteinuria.

list.title: Impaired filtration:
list.snippet: Damaged glomeruli can't filter blood as effectively, leading to a buildup of waste products and excess fluid in the body.

list.title: High blood pressure:
list.snippet: Diabetes often leads to high blood pressure, which further damages the kidneys and accelerates the progression of kidney disease.

list.title: Kidney failure:
list.snippet: If left untreated, diabetic nephropathy can worsen over time, potentially leading to kidney failure, requiring dialysis or a transplant.
Early stages often have no noticeable symptoms.
As kidney disease progresses, symptoms may include:
High blood pressure that becomes harder to control.
Swelling in the feet, ankles, hands, or face.
Foamy urine.
Fatigue, general unwell feeling.
Loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting.
Shortness of breath.
Itching.
Confusion or difficulty thinking.

list.title: Blood sugar control:
list.snippet: Keeping blood sugar levels within the target range is crucial for slowing or preventing kidney damage.

list.title: Blood pressure control:
list.snippet: Managing high blood pressure is also vital for protecting the kidneys.

list.title: ACE inhibitors and ARBs:
list.snippet: These blood pressure medications can help protect the kidneys from further damage.

list.title: Regular checkups:
list.snippet: Annual urine tests to check for microalbuminuria (small amounts of protein in the urine) can help detect kidney damage early.

list.title: Lifestyle modifications:
list.snippet: Healthy diet, regular exercise, and weight management can help control blood sugar and blood pressure.

list.title: Consultation with healthcare professionals:
list.snippet: Patients should work with their doctors, including nephrologists and dieticians, to develop a personalized management plan.
